modules.name: Array
modules.header:
A run of elements whose length is fixed when it is made and whose storage is on the heap.
`Array<T>` is what to reach for when the length is decided at run time and never changes afterwards. It is not
`T[N]`, whose length is part of its type and whose storage is wherever the value containing it lives; it is not
`T[..]`, which borrows storage someone else owns; and it is not `Vector<T>`, which can grow. Owning storage of
a length chosen at run time is the one thing none of the others does.
An array owns its storage and its elements, so copying is prohibited and it is move-only. Handing one to a function
requires an explicit move; reading the source afterwards is rejected while
compiling rather than discovered later. Destruction destroys every element and then releases the block, in that
order, so an array of things that own something does not leak what they own.
The allocator is injected at construction and kept. An array made from one allocator is released to the same one,
which is what lets an arena's arrays disappear with the arena and a pool's come back to the pool.
Every constructor copies its elements into the storage. A move-only element type cannot be copied, so an array of
those has to be built another way — `Vector<T>` and its `Push` is the shape that works, since each element is
moved in exactly once.

modules.name: Capacity
modules.header:
Overflow-checked sizing arithmetic, shared by every container in this package so the checks exist once rather than
once per type.
Integer overflow wraps silently, so `count * sizeof(T)` is the single most dangerous expression a container
writes: a product that wraps asks the allocator for a small block and then writes far past it. Every allocation in
this package sizes itself through `ByteSize` rather than multiplying inline.
The checks are written out rather than reached for from `Core`, because each of these does something beyond the
arithmetic — choosing a growth, falling back when a doubling does not fit — and a checked multiply is one line
of that. What matters is that the dangerous product is never evaluated: `ByteSize` divides instead.
These fail with a `CollectionError` like the public operations that call them, and return their result only when
the arithmetic holds.
Internal helpers; not part of the package API.

modules.name: CollectionError
modules.header:
Why a collection operation could not be completed.
Every case is a failure: an operation that can fail returns its result, or nothing, through `T ! CollectionError`.
The return type is what separates the two kinds of failure in this package: an operation returning a native
fallible needed memory or capacity arithmetic, while an operation returning an optional or a `bool` never
allocates and has exactly one way to fail. So an exhausted allocator can never be mistaken for a missing key, and a
rejected index can never be mistaken for either.
One rule holds everywhere: a failure means the receiver is unchanged. A container that could not
grow is the container it was, with the same elements at the same indices, and a caller may retry, give up, or
carry on using it. Nothing here leaves a collection half-modified.

modules.name: Comparing
modules.header:
Ready-made ordering callbacks for the key types an ordered container is usually keyed on.
A tree takes its comparison as a function for the reason a table takes its hash as one: Rux has no closures, and
an interface value would be stored and dispatched through at every step of every descent — a dozen indirect calls
for a lookup that should be a dozen compares.
An ordering is one answer rather than two calls, which is why these return `Ordering` and not a pair of `<` and
`==` predicates. A descent asks one question per node and branches three ways on the answer.
A caller keying on a type not listed here writes its own. The rules are the ordinary ones: the comparison must be
consistent, must be the same every call, and must agree with equality — two keys that compare `Equal` are one key
as far as a tree is concerned, and the second one to arrive replaces the first.

modules.name: ContainerStorage
modules.header:
Talking to an allocator in elements rather than bytes.
Every container here holds a run of `T` and needs three things from an allocator: storage for a count of them,
storage of a different count with the old contents carried over, and the storage given back. Doing that by hand
means computing a layout at each site, and a layout computed wrongly is the defect that writes past the end of a
block the allocator thought was smaller. These helpers exist so it is computed once.
The layout comes from `sizeof(T)` and `alignof(T)`, asked of the element type at each instantiation. That is what
makes these usable by a container that has never seen an element and has none to hand: nothing here needs a sample
value.
A count of zero is not an error. It asks the allocator for a zero-sized block, which every allocator here answers
with a shared non-null aligned address, so an empty container is not a special shape and needs no null checks
downstream. That block must still be released, exactly like any other.
Internal to this package, and package-private so that it stays that way: these are the plumbing every container
shares, not something a caller reaches for. What a caller reaches for is a container, and what the plumbing does
is visible through one — a zero-sized element, a growth the allocator refuses, and the destruction of everything
held all show up at that surface, which is where Tests/Packages/Collections/ContainerStorage checks them.

modules.name: Deque
modules.header:
A double-ended queue over a circular buffer.
Elements go on and come off at either end in constant time, which is what a vector cannot offer at the front:
shifting every element along costs a linear pass per removal. This is the queue — `PushBack` and `PopFront` are
first in, first out — as `Vector` is the stack.
The capacity is always a power of two, or zero. That is what lets the ring wrap with a mask rather than a
division: logical element `i` lives at physical `(head + i) & (capacity - 1)`. Because the elements can straddle
the end of the block, a deque cannot always hand out one contiguous view; `AsSlices` gives the two runs without
moving anything, and `MakeContiguous` rotates them back together where one view is what a caller needs.
A deque owns its storage and its elements, so copying is prohibited and it is move-only. The allocator is
injected at construction and kept. Destruction destroys every element it holds and then releases the block.
Every operation that can fail leaves the deque exactly as it was. Growth allocates a fresh block, relocates the
elements into it, and only then releases the old one, so a refused allocation costs nothing at all — not even the
wrapped layout the elements were in.

modules.name: HashMap
modules.header:
An associative table: keys to values, in no particular order, with constant expected time for everything.
Built on the `Table` kernel, so the probing, the displacement and the deletion are described there rather than
here. What this adds is the pair of callbacks that give a key type its identity, and the operations a caller
actually names.
The hash and equality are supplied rather than taken from the key type, because Rux has no closures and an
interface value would be stored and dispatched through on every lookup. `Hashing` has ready-made pairs for the
usual key types; a caller keying on its own type writes them, and the one rule is that keys comparing equal must
hash the same.
The hash is seeded, and the seed is drawn from `Rux/Entropy` unless the caller supplies one. That is what stops an
adversary who chooses keys from computing a few thousand that collide and turning every lookup into a scan.
A map owns its keys and values, so it prohibits copying and is move-only. Entries are destroyed when the map is,
when they are cleared, and when they are replaced — but not when they are removed, which hands the value back
instead.

modules.name: HashSet
modules.header:
A set of distinct values, in no particular order, with constant expected time for everything.
The same `Table` kernel as `HashMap`, with nothing stored alongside each key. A set is a map whose values carry no
information, and saying so in the type rather than duplicating the probing is what keeps the two in step: a fix to
the displacement or the deletion is a fix to both.
The hash and equality are supplied for the same reason they are there, and the seed is drawn the same way.
A set owns its elements, so it prohibits copying and is move-only.

modules.name: Hashing
modules.header:
Ready-made hash and equality callbacks for the key types a table is usually keyed on.
A table takes its hash as a function rather than through an interface, because Rux has no closures and an
interface value would have to be stored and dispatched through per lookup. The signature carries the table's seed
alongside the key, which is what makes the hashing randomized: two tables in one program hash the same key
differently, and neither is predictable to anyone who has not seen the seed.
Every hash here is `SipHash`, which is the one in `Rux/Hash` designed for exactly this. An adversary who chooses
keys can find collisions in any of the others by hand, and a table full of colliding keys is a table whose every
lookup is a linear scan — a denial of service against anything keyed on input it did not write. `SipHash` makes
finding those collisions as hard as guessing the seed.
A caller keying on a type not listed here writes the pair itself: a hash that reads the whole key and mixes the
seed in, and an equality that agrees with it. The one rule is the usual one — two keys that compare equal must
hash the same.

modules.name: Iteration
modules.header:
Walking a run of contiguous elements, which every container in this package can hand out a view of.
The compiler drives a `for` loop by shape: anything with a `Next` returning an `Option` is an iterator, and the
item type is whatever that option carries. That leaves the choice of item to the iterator, and there are three
worth having.
`ValueIterator` yields elements by copy, which is what reading a sequence of numbers wants and what a move-only
element type must not be walked with — copying one would give two owners to a value that promises one.
`ReferenceIterator` yields a pointer to each element, which works for any element type at all and is how a
move-only one is read without being moved.
`MutableReferenceIterator` yields a writable pointer to each element, allowing in-place changes without copying.
All three borrow. None owns the storage it walks, and none may outlive the container it came from or survive that
container growing, rehashing or being freed — which is the one thing about iteration in this package worth
remembering.
A consuming iterator, which moves elements out of a container and leaves it empty, belongs to the container that
can be emptied rather than here.

modules.name: Presentation
modules.header:
Showing what a sequential container holds, without disturbing it.
A container cannot implement `Debug` itself: what a `Vector<T>` looks like is entirely a question about `T`, and
an interface implementation has nowhere to say "when the element can be shown". So these are handwritten
functions carrying the bound — `WriteVectorDebug<T: Debug>` — which is the shape the language does have. Each
instantiation resolves its element's `WriteDebug` at compile time; nothing is dispatched at run time.
They borrow, and that is the whole design. A container owns its elements and hands out no copies of a move-only
one, so a diagnostic that took an element out to print it would be taking ownership of it — which is exactly what
a caller with a container they still need cannot afford. Every element here is shown through a borrow of it, so a
vector of a move-only type can be written as many times as wanted and still holds everything afterwards.
A vector and an array are one run of elements, so both hand `Rux/Text` their slice and it does the rest. A deque
is the exception, and the reason is its shape rather than an oversight: its elements live in a ring, so a deque
that has wrapped holds them in two runs with a gap between. It writes them as one sequence — which is what they
are to a reader — by walking both runs inside one pair of brackets, which is the one thing the slice writer
cannot be asked to do.
Maps and sets are here too, written `{key: value, key: value}` and `{element, element}` — braces rather than
brackets, because what a map holds is not a run of things and reading one as a sequence would be reading it
wrongly. The two kinds differ in exactly one respect, and it is the only interesting question they raise.
An ordered map or set is written in key order, which is the order it keeps and the order every walk of it takes,
so its rendering is a fact about its contents and nothing else. A hash map or set is written in the order of its
table, which is a fact about the container rather than about what it holds: it follows from the seed drawn when
the container was made and from every insertion and removal since, because displacement decides which of two
entries that want the same slot gets it. So two containers holding exactly the same entries render differently,
and so does the same container in the next run of the same program. That is documented rather than fixed: sorting
would need an ordering on the key that a hash container does not have and was built not to need, and inventing
one would make every hash container require something extra just so that its diagnostic looked tidy. A caller who
needs a stable order has an ordered map.
`CollectionError` presents itself here as well, for the same reason the containers do — this package depends on
`Rux/Text` and Text does not depend on it, so this is the side of the edge the implementation can live on.
`Display` is the description a reader is shown and `Debug` names the case, exactly as for the errors Text
presents. The descriptions are stable and are not a parsing contract: a program branches on the case.

modules.name: Table
modules.header:
The open-addressing kernel `HashMap` and `HashSet` are both built on, so the probe sequence, the displacement rule
and the deletion exist once rather than twice.
**Robin Hood.** Every entry records how far it sits from the slot its hash names — its probe distance. An
insertion that meets an entry closer to home than itself takes the slot and carries that entry onward, so the
distances along a chain never decrease and the worst one stays near the average. That is what keeps a lookup
bounded even when a table is nearly full, where plain linear probing degrades into a long scan of somebody else's
chain.
It also makes a miss cheap. A search that reaches a slot whose occupant is closer to home than the search has
travelled can stop there: the key it is looking for would have taken that slot on the way past. No tombstone, no
scan to the end of the chain.
**Backward-shift deletion.** Removing an entry moves the following ones back one slot each, stopping at an empty
slot or one already at home. That leaves the table exactly as if the removed entry had never been inserted --
there are no tombstones here at all, so a table that is churned rather than grown does not slowly fill with them
and rehash for no reason.
**Randomized hashing.** The hash a table uses is seeded, and the seed is a secret drawn from `Rux/Entropy`.
Without it, an adversary who chooses keys can compute a few thousand that collide and turn every lookup linear,
which is a denial of service against anything keying a table on input it did not write. The seeded hashers in
`Hashing` use `SipHash`, which is what makes guessing the seed the only way in.
Occupancy lives in the distance byte rather than in the key, so there is no reserved or sentinel key: every
possible `K` is storable, including zero and `uint::Max` and any struct bit pattern.
Internal to this package: the kernel, not something a caller reaches for.

modules.name: Tree
modules.header:
The red-black kernel `TreeMap` and `TreeSet` are both built on, so the rotations and the two fix-ups exist once
rather than twice.
A red-black tree keeps its entries in order and its height within twice the best possible, by colouring each node
and holding to four rules: the root is black, a red node has no red child, every path from a node down to a
missing child crosses the same number of black nodes, and a missing child counts as black. Insertion and removal
each break one of those locally, and each has a fix-up that walks back up until it is true again.
What that buys over a hash table is order. A tree walks its entries smallest first, answers what the least key
above a bound is, and never rehashes — so a walk stays meaningful across insertions in a way a table's cannot,
since a table moves entries between slots whenever it grows. What it costs is a pointer chase per level and an
allocation per entry, against the table's single run of memory and constant expected time. Reach for the tree when
order is part of the question, and the table when it is not.
Each node is its own allocation, which is what lets a node keep its address while the tree is rearranged around
it. Removal relinks the successor rather than copying its contents over the removed node, so the entry that stays
keeps the address it had. A table cannot promise that at all.
Every comparison goes through a function the caller supplies, for the reason the hash tables take theirs: Rux has
no closures, and an interface would be dispatched through at every step of every descent.
Internal to this package: the kernel, not something a caller reaches for.

modules.name: TreeMap
modules.header:
A map that keeps its keys in order.
`HashMap` is the one to reach for by default: it answers a lookup in constant expected time and this one takes a
pointer chase per level. What this offers instead is order. It walks its entries smallest key first, answers what
the nearest key above or below a bound is, and hands back everything between two bounds — none of which a hash
table can do at all, since a hash scatters keys on purpose and moves them between slots whenever it grows.
The ordering is the caller's, given once as a function and used for every descent. It has to be consistent, the
same every call, and agree with equality: two keys that compare `Equal` are one key here, and the second to
arrive replaces the first's value. `Comparing` has ready-made ones for the usual key types.
The balancing, the node ownership and the ordered walk are `Tree`'s; this is the map's shape over them.

modules.name: TreeSet
modules.header:
A set that keeps its elements in order.
`HashSet` answers membership in constant expected time and is the one to reach for by default. This one costs a
pointer chase per level and gives back order: it walks smallest first, answers what the nearest element above or
below a bound is, and hands back everything between two bounds. A hash set can do none of that, because a hash
scatters elements on purpose.
Order also changes what the algebra costs. Two hash sets can only be compared by looking every element of one up
in the other; two ordered sets could be merged in one pass. That merge is not what runs here — the predicates
below still ask `Contains` per element — because a merge needs both walks to survive the other's removals, and
what it would save is a logarithm. The operations that change a set do exploit the order, by asking for the next
element by key rather than by pointer, which is what lets them remove while walking.
The elements are the keys of a tree whose values are nothing at all. The unit `()` occupies no bytes, so a set is
a map with the values compiled away rather than a second copy of the same balancing.
An element must be copyable, for the same reason a `HashSet`'s must: the comparison takes its two elements by
value, and every descent compares against elements the set is holding. An element that owned something would be
handed to the comparison and destroyed there, taking what it owned with it. A set of owning values needs a
comparison that borrows, and there is no way to spell one that also works for the copyable case; until there is,
put the owning values in a `TreeMap` under keys that are copyable.

modules.name: Vector
modules.header:
A contiguous run of elements that grows as things are appended to it.
`Vector<T>` is the container to reach for by default. It is the stack — `Push` and `TryPop` work at the end that
costs nothing to reach — and it is what a sequence of unknown length is built into before anything else looks at
it. `Array<T>` is what it becomes when the length stops changing.
A vector owns its storage and its elements, so copying is prohibited and it is move-only. Handing one to a function
requires an explicit move. Destruction destroys every element it
holds and then releases the block; the spare capacity past the length holds nothing and is not touched.
The allocator is injected at construction and kept, so a vector built from an arena disappears with the arena.
Capacity doubles rather than growing by a constant, which is what makes a run of appends cost an amortized
constant each rather than a reallocation every time. Capacity is never reduced except by `ShrinkToFit`, so a
vector that has been large stays cheap to refill.
`Push` moves its argument in rather than copying it, so a vector is how a sequence of elements that own something
is built: each is moved in exactly once and destroyed exactly once, when the vector is.
Two failure shapes, as everywhere in this package: an operation that may allocate reports a `CollectionError`, and
one that cannot allocate reports an ordinary miss with a `bool` and an out-parameter. A reported failure means the
vector is exactly as it was.

doc.summary: Why a collection operation could not be completed.
doc.markdown:
Why a collection operation could not be completed.
Every case means the operation did not happen and the collection is as it was.

cases.name: OutOfMemory
cases.doc:
The allocator had no storage to give.
Transient in principle: the same request may succeed later, and a caller with something to release may make
it so.

cases.name: CapacityOverflow
cases.doc:
The size the operation needed could not be represented.
A count times an element size that does not fit in a `uint`, or a length plus a growth that wraps. Not a
shortage of memory but of arithmetic: no allocator could have served the request, because the number naming
it does not exist.

cases.name: IndexOutOfRange
cases.doc: The index was not one the collection has.

cases.name: Unsupported
cases.doc:
The allocator refused the layout itself rather than running short.
An alignment stricter than the allocator serves, or a block it did not hand out. Retrying is pointless: the
same request will be refused the same way.

members.name: IsTransient
members.signature: pub func IsTransient(self: CollectionError) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether the same operation might succeed later.
doc.markdown:
Whether the same operation might succeed later.
`self` is borrowed. True only for `OutOfMemory`, which says the allocator had nothing to give rather than
that the request was impossible. A capacity that cannot be represented will not start being representable,
an index the collection does not have will not appear, and a layout the allocator refuses will be refused
again.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: whether trying again could succeed

Writes the description of why an operation did not happen, or `no error` for success.
The five cases stay distinguishable in words as they are in the type: a shortage of memory is not a size that
cannot be named, and neither is a layout the allocator refuses outright. Those distinctions decide whether a
caller retries, so a description that blurred them would send somebody to fix the wrong thing.
The descriptions are stable. They are not a parsing contract: a program branches on the case.
Reports whatever the writer reported, and `UnsupportedRequest` for any style or precision.

doc.summary: Writes a borrowed hash map as `{key: value, key: value}`.
doc.markdown:
Writes a borrowed hash map as `{key: value, key: value}`.
An empty map is `{}`. Braces rather than brackets, because a map is not a run of elements and reading its
rendering as one would be reading it wrongly.
The order is the table's, which follows from the seed the map was made with and from every insertion and removal
since — so it is not the insertion order, it does not hold between two maps with the same entries, and it changes
between runs of the same program. Nothing here sorts, since that would need an ordering on the key that a hash
map does not have. `TreeMap` is the container whose rendering is stable.
Every key and value is shown through a borrow of it, so a map of move-only entries is shown without taking one
out. `spec` is handed to each of them unchanged.
Reports whatever the writer or an entry's implementation reported, stopping at the first refusal.

doc.summary: Puts `key` and `value` into the tree, replacing the value already stored under an equal key.
doc.markdown:
Puts `key` and `value` into the tree, replacing the value already stored under an equal key.
Takes ownership of both. Hands back the value an equal key already had, or `none` when the key is new — so a
caller learns whether anything was displaced without a lookup first, and gets the displaced value rather than
having it quietly destroyed. When the key is already present the new key is destroyed rather than stored, since
the one in the tree is equal to it and is what everything already hanging below it was ordered against.
Reports `OutOfMemory` when the node cannot be allocated, having changed nothing — but `key` and `value` are
destroyed rather than handed back, because there is nowhere left to put them.
Runs in time proportional to the height, with at most two rotations. Allocates one node for a new key and
nothing at all for one already present.

members.name: IntoArray
members.signature: pub func IntoArray(self: Vector<T>) -> Array<T> ! CollectionError

doc.summary: Hands the storage itself to a fixed-length array, copying nothing.
doc.markdown:
Hands the storage itself to a fixed-length array, copying nothing.
Consumes the vector. The spare capacity is trimmed first, and the trim has to succeed: an array releases its
block with the layout of its length, so a block still carrying spare capacity would be given back under a layout
it was not taken with.
A failed trim is a failed transfer, and the vector is gone either way — it was consumed by the call — so
its elements are destroyed and an empty array comes back. That costs the elements, which is why it is
reported rather than silent; a shrink refused by an allocator is close to impossible, since it asks for less
than it already holds.
doc.returns: an array taking the vector's storage rather than copying it

An iterator that takes a vector apart, yielding each element by value.
Move-only: it owns the storage the vector owned, prohibits copying, and destroys it with `~VectorIntoIterator`.
This is how a vector of elements that
own something is emptied into somewhere else — each element is moved out rather than copied, and whatever is
left when the iterator's life ends is destroyed with it.
